title: A REST call and a row, one SELECT apart
description: HTTP Client closes the smallest possible gap between a [REST API](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110) and a DuckDB row: instead of standing up a Python or Node.js sidecar to fetch a payload and load it back in, you call a scalar function inside a `SELECT` and get the response as a [`JSON`](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/json/json_functions) value you can extract, cast, and join on the spot. That tight coupling is its whole reason to exist — and also the source of every caveat below. It is built for ad-hoc API calls and low-volume per-row enrichment, not for high-throughput or streaming integrations.

sections.title: How it works
sections.description: The extension is a deliberately thin SQL surface over a single synchronous HTTP request — there is no `ATTACH`, no connection pool and no background fetcher. Each function call issues the request, blocks until the full response is in memory, and returns it as a JSON value. On the DuckDB 2.0 build the request goes through DuckDB's own HTTP stack (the [httpfs](https://duckdb.org/docs/extensions/httpfs/overview) extension for `https://`), so DuckDB's HTTP settings and HTTP secrets apply. The result composes cleanly into CTEs, lateral joins, and `CREATE TABLE AS` — anywhere a scalar JSON value is acceptable.

bulletPoints.label: Synchronous and blocking
bulletPoints.description: DuckDB stalls on each call until the response arrives or the request fails. On DuckDB 2.0 the timeout is DuckDB's `http_timeout` setting (connect and read, default 30 s), failed idempotent requests are retried per `http_retries`, and a query can be interrupted between rows. A slow endpoint still slows the whole query.

bulletPoints.label: One call per row
bulletPoints.description: Per-row enrichment issues exactly one HTTP request per input row, sequentially, with no connection reuse exposed at the SQL layer. Fine for tens or hundreds of rows; for tens of thousands it is slow and very likely to get rate-limited upstream. Pre-aggregate to distinct keys or cache responses into a table with [`CREATE TABLE AS`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/create_table) before joining at scale.

bulletPoints.label: JSON response struct
bulletPoints.description: Every call returns a JSON object shaped `{status, reason, body}` — plus `headers` (the response headers as an object) on DuckDB 2.0. `status` is the numeric HTTP code, `reason` is the [HTTP reason phrase](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#name-status-codes), and `body` is a string (base64 with `body_encoding: "base64"` when it is not UTF-8, on 2.0). Pull fields out with [`->>`](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/json/json_functions); to drill into a JSON response body, cast it first: `((res->>'body')::JSON)->>'$.field'`.

bulletPoints.label: Headers and params are MAPs
bulletPoints.description: Headers and POST parameters are passed as DuckDB [`MAP`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/data_types/map) literals — `MAP{'key': 'value', ...}`. Headers go on the wire as-is; how the params map is encoded into the body (JSON vs. URL-encoded form) depends on which POST function you call.

sections.title: Scope and caveats
sections.description: Read this before pointing it at production traffic — for anything it lacks (streaming, client certificates, parallel fan-out), keep a real HTTP client or shell out to `curl` via [shellfs](/products/extensions/shellfs).

bulletPoints.label: Experimental status
bulletPoints.description: Marked **experimental** by the [upstream README](https://github.com/Query-farm/duckdb-extension-httpclient) — "USE AT YOUR OWN RISK!". Pin a known-good extension version in any pipeline that depends on it.

bulletPoints.label: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, HEAD
bulletPoints.description: `GET`, `HEAD` and `POST` (JSON or form-encoded) on every build; `PUT` and `DELETE` on the DuckDB 2.0 build. There is no `PATCH` (DuckDB's HTTP layer has no PATCH request) — for that, shell out to `curl` via [shellfs](/products/extensions/shellfs).

bulletPoints.label: Buffered responses
bulletPoints.description: The entire response body is buffered into memory; on DuckDB 2.0 a body larger than `http_client_max_response_size` (default 100 MiB) raises an error. Prefer shellfs + `curl` piped through [`read_csv`](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/csv/overview) / [`read_json`](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/json/loading_json.html) when a response is too big to hold in memory.

bulletPoints.label: Credentials are visible in the query plan
bulletPoints.description: Any token or secret inlined into a `headers` or `params` map appears in the cached query plan and `EXPLAIN` output. Source credentials from the environment with [`getenv`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/functions/utility#getenv) and bind them through [`SET VARIABLE`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/set) — `getenv` resolves at parse time, so the literal value never lands in a cached plan or session log. On DuckDB 2.0 you can instead keep a bearer token or extra headers in an [HTTP secret](https://duckdb.org/docs/extensions/httpfs/https#authenticating) scoped to the API's URL.

bulletPoints.label: Sandboxed (DuckDB 2.0)
bulletPoints.description: Every function refuses to send a request when `enable_external_access` is false. Redirects are re-checked hop by hop: `https://` is never downgraded to `http://`, and `Authorization`/`Cookie` headers are not forwarded to another host.
